I Studied $17,684,592 in YouTube Sales. Here's What Actually Makes Money...

You see, my venture capital for creators, Eyeball VC has tracked $17,684,592 in revenue for business owners on YouTube, and they shared their biggest findings with me. Here are the 3 biggest levers you can pull today to make more money.

𝗟𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝟭: 𝗦𝘁𝗼𝗽 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘄𝘀.

The first lever any business or creator can pull is reframing what actually matters on YouTube. You have been told a thousand different things about what moves the needle. "Get as many views as possible." "Go super niche." Here is what the actual data says.

The 100 most viewed videos out of thousands tracked accounted for only 11% of total revenue. On average those 100 videos took more time and money to make than everything else, and they still returned just 11% of the money. So "get as many views as possible" is not accurate when it comes to what moves revenue, outside of general awareness.

The reasons those videos fail to convert are where it gets interesting.

The first reason is memetic copying and ego. Most creators watch the top 20% of their space pull roughly 80% of the views, and on the surface they read that as more views equals success. So they copy the same formats, spend the same time and money, and post the same volume, in both lifestyle and educational content. The ego piece runs underneath it. Business owner types tend to be wired for competition, and fewer views feels like losing. When losing gets tied to self worth, people start chasing views for the sake of views instead of building content that converts. High view content can absolutely convert, but the view chasers never stop to understand why a video converts on the back end, so the views climb and the sales do not follow.

The second reason is content strategy. Some videos exist to pull new viewers into your ecosystem. They are the lowest common denominator, built for the broadest possible audience, so they naturally attract people with low or no buying intent. They rack up outlier view counts while bringing in the wrong audience, or an audience that is nowhere near ready to buy. This is not always bad, because you always need new viewers coming in. It just is not where the money is.

So unless you have a reason beyond revenue, maximizing views is usually not how you approach back end conversion. There is nuance to it, but the data is overwhelming, and the rule of thumb holds: chasing views is rarely the most direct path to cash unlike the next lever which is the most direct path to cash.

𝗟𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝟮: 𝗙𝗶𝘅 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗳𝗿𝗮𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗴.

Views are not the lever. Titles are, because a title positions both you and the viewer.
To understand why titles matter this much, you have to see what an unoptimized title looks like. For revenue, the worst offender is the "how to" title. These titles set out to solve the viewer's problem, and that is exactly why they fail to make money. 

The data is brutal. "How to" titles pull 32% of all tracked clicks but only 18% of all revenue. A third of every tracked click on the platform, returning under a fifth of the money.
It gets worse. If the viewer applies what you taught, they no longer need you. If they apply it and fail, they churn out even harder and never come back. It can work, but it is a multi year play built on cashing in trust and reciprocity, not sustainable cash flow.
The fix is simple, and it is all framing. "How to" sells poorly. "How I" sells. 

It works because a first person video does not hand over the solution. It removes limiting beliefs, because the viewer watches someone who already did the thing they want to do. And it is instant social proof. 

𝗟𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝟯: 𝗚𝗲𝘁 𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗰.

Framing gets you most of the way. You push a title further by making it first person, outcome focused, and specific.

A first person outcome title lives or dies on specificity, and that means exact dollar amounts, ideally as a rate. Vague first person titles like "My journey" or "A day in my life" earn nothing. A flat zero, even though they are first person, because they carry no specificity.

A killer title looks like this: "I Make $8,300 A Month From One Email List I Almost Deleted." That one is remixed from a real winning title that prints daily, changed to protect the creator and his strategy. It is first person, but it is also loaded with an exact dollar amount and a rate. Titles with exact dollar amounts pull 34% of clicks and 52% of revenue.
